record.paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
record.context_brief: Explicit atomic density functionals and variational principles
record.original_question: Can explicit functionals of a topological atom’s one-electron density, or a successful variational principle based on that density or another atomic function, be constructed so that topological-atom properties can be computed rather than only formally asserted to exist?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a non-relativistic Born–Oppenheimer molecular system described by an N-electron wavefunction Ψ on configuration space, with one-electron density
  ρ(r) = N ∫ |Ψ(r, x_2, …, x_N)|^2 dx_2 ⋯ dx_N.
A "topological atom" Ω is a region of three-dimensional space bounded by a surface S(Ω) of zero flux of ∇ρ, i.e. ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0 for all r ∈ S(Ω), where n(r) is the outward unit normal. Associated with Ω one defines atomic property values M_Ω (e.g. atomic energy, kinetic energy, electron population, multipole moments) as integrals of corresponding property densities over Ω, and an "atomic state" object encoding the restriction of the system to Ω.

Problem. Do either of the following constructions exist?

(a) Explicit density functional. Construct an explicit, computable functional F_Ω[ρ] taking as input only the one-electron density ρ (restricted to Ω, or the global ρ together with the zero-flux boundary), such that
  M_Ω = F_Ω[ρ]
for a chosen nontrivial atomic property M_Ω, with F_Ω given in closed analytic form rather than only being asserted to exist via an existence argument.

(b) Variational principle for the topological atom. Construct a variational (or stationary-action) principle whose input is the one-electron density ρ on Ω—or some other single-particle atomic function f defined on Ω—and whose Euler–Lagrange equations or stationary value yield, in a constructive way, the atomic properties M_Ω of the topological atom. The principle must be strong enough that knowledge of the optimizing ρ (or f) actually determines M_Ω, rather than only characterizing Ω implicitly through the zero-flux condition.

Decide whether such an F_Ω[ρ] in (a) and/or such a variational principle in (b) can be constructed, and exhibit one if it can.
artifact.category_tag: Density functionals for QTAIM topological atoms
artifact.status_search_result: Available literature on QTAIM indicates that, while subsystem variational/stationary-action derivations exist (Schrödinger- and Schwinger-based formulations), no explicit closed-form functional of the one-electron density yielding atomic properties of a topological atom has been constructed; the link to DFT remains formal. No constructive variational principle on the density (or another atomic function) that determines M_Ω has been established. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Revisiting the variational nature of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules
status_evidence.snippet: A simplified derivation of the variational nature of the real space basins used in QTAIM, clarifying non-standard characteristics of the variational problem.
status_evidence.claim: Variational treatments of topological atoms exist but have non-standard features that are easily misinterpreted, and do not yield explicit density functionals for atomic properties.

status_evidence.title: Toward the multi-component quantum theory of atoms in molecules: a variational derivation
status_evidence.snippet: Extended subsystem variational procedure inspired by Schrödinger's variational principle, derives surface terms via flux of current property densities.
status_evidence.claim: Existing subsystem variational derivations produce surface flux conditions but no explicit density-only functional for M_Ω.

status_evidence.title: Some notes on: What is an Atom in a Molecule
status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of open problems in foundations of QTAIM, including absence of explicit density functional for topological atoms and lack of successful density-based variational principle.
status_evidence.claim: The construction of an explicit density functional or successful density-based variational principle for topological atoms is identified as an unresolved foundational issue.
